newsitem.title: COTE D'IVOIRE: FEATURE-Welcome to Liberian refugee Peacetown.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Welcome to Liberian refugee Peacetown.

text.p: A group of survivors from Liberia's bloody civil war have thrived since establishing their own settlement in neighbouring Ivory Coast, appropriately called Peacetown.
With tiny mud huts and rooftops made from woven palms leaves and decorated with flowers, Peacetown has come to symbolise the resilience of refugees from Liberia's six-year-old conflict.

"We have all that can keep body and soul in unity," says Isaac Collins, the chairman of an eight-man governing council for the settlement near Guiglo, 400 km (240 miles) northwest of the Ivorian commercial capital of Abidjan.
Peacetown's residents are the survivors of an attack last year in Liberia that killed 32 of their number.
Refugees are all smiles as they welcome visitors as if to erase the memory of the day in June 1995 when rebels of the Liberia Peace Council attacked Tai village, 80 km (50 miles) south of Guiglo.
A bold signpost proudly proclaims "Welcome to Peacetown."
The main problem for the refugees is healthcare which is expensive despite a medical centre run by the non-governmental organisation Africare and drugs sold to refugees at half the market price.
Half price is still expensive, Peacetown dwellers say.
"We have lost so many brothers and sisters over the past one year because of lack of means to take care of our medical bills," laments Julie Brooks.
"Whenever someone falls ill and is rushed to hospital, he or she is subjected to pay upfront for medication before being attended to," chairman Collins complains.
Health personnel assigned to the settlement by the International Committee of the Red Cross and Africare are not enough for the task, he says.
"When it comes to health matters, which as you know is a damn expensive aspect of life, we are greatly lacking," he added.
Liberians face more problems with aid agencies scaling down on numbers of refugees to get handouts to "the most vulnerable."
Last August only 178,000 benefitted from 1,200 tonnes of supplies compared with 247,000 who received 1,680 tonnes of material before the decision to slash handouts.
"By next January, the number of beneficiaries would drop to 118,000 and only 810 tonnes would be supplied," said Janick Ferrier, the regional delegate of the Red Cross in Guiglo.

Collins' compound has an open cabin where meetings are held. At night the villagers live with the faint light from lanterns while in the small market the women display vegetables and bananas harvested from their makeshift farms and gardens.

Small eateries with exotic names like "Silver and Gold Restaurant" and "Kings and Queens" abound serving Liberian dishes such as "palavar sauce", "potato green soup" and "cassava leaves" to accompany Liberia's cherished staple rice.
In typical West African fashion, churches of various denominations -- Catholic, Baptist, Lutheran, Methodist -- have sprang up all round Peacetown.
"It is because there are so many souls to be saved," says Reverend Alexander Gee of the Lutheran church as he points to his white painted chapel yet to be adorned with a cross.
"When the war began we were always with our handbags ready to return anytime that there is any sign of a lasting and peaceful atmosphere in Liberia," he said.
"But so far none of us seem to think this will happen," he added.
Civil war erupted in Africa's oldest republic on Christmas eve in 1989 when the faction of chief warlord Charles Taylor invaded Liberia from Ivory Coast.

Since then the southwestern region of Ivory Coast alone has received more than 350,000 refugees out of the nearly 750,000 declared by the United Nations from the Liberian conflict to be scattered throughout West Africa.
The number of Liberians in Ivory Coast's southwestern border towns are estimated to outnumber the local population.
The refugees are in no hurry to leave their new settlement as peace has failed to return to Liberia despite numerous ceasefire accords.
"With the Ivorian government blessings to allow us settle here, I am afraid none of us would want to return in the immediate future," said Reverend Gee.
The refugees have just completed a primary school for the children in Peacetown which Collins said with confidence would open soon "by the grace of God".
